en: Vimānavatthu: The Mansion of the Man,
Chapter on Well-Placed [Offerings]
10. The Story of the Serīsaka Mansion:
“Listen to how the meeting between the yakkha and the merchants took place at that time.”
And how it was, even in its various details—
listen all of you to that well-spoken account.
There was once a king named Pāyāsi.
Having attained companionship with the earth-dwellers, he, glorious and superhuman,
while rejoicing in his own celestial mansion,
addressed the human beings.
“In a crooked forest, a place uninhabited by humans,
in a wilderness devoid of water and lacking food,
in the midst of a difficult path through the jungle— ”
People, their minds ruined by fear, pursue crookedness.
Here there are no fruits that consist of roots, and there is no grasping;
whence, then, could there be food?
Except for dust and sand, and for parched,
hot, and dreadful sands; like a heated skull in a desert wasteland.
Free from hardship, equal to the world beyond,
this ancient dwelling of the greedy is a region of the earth that appears like a battlefield.
Now, for what reason and desiring what have you entered this place together and gathered here so suddenly?
“Out of greed, fear, or indeed through delusion.
“Caravan leaders from Magadha and Aṅga,
having loaded various kinds of merchandise;”
Seeking wealth and hoping for gain,
they journeyed to the land of Sindhu-Sovīra;
unable to endure thirst even by day, they traveled on.
Considering our fitness and compassion for one another,
let us all proceed with this speed;
we have set out on the road at night, at an improper time.
Those two-footed ones, having strayed from the path,
blind and bewildered, lost in the forest;
in the midst of a difficult-to-traverse jungle track—
"Confused in mind, we did not know the direction.
But now that we have seen this, never seen before—
the most excellent celestial mansion and yourself, O Yakkha— "
“Anticipating a life even longer than that,
they saw him and were thrilled, joyful, and elated.
“The beauty of this shore of the ocean, and...”
Go for the sake of wealth to the dwellings of hunters, to roads and paths,
to rivers and difficult mountain passes, and to many different directions.
Beholding the victory of others over the men of Verañjā,
whatever you have heard or even seen, O Pakkhandiyas, [tell it].
“‘We hear of that wonder from you, dear ones.
‘Even more wonderful than this, O Prince,
is something we have neither heard nor seen:’”
Having seen all this, which surpasses that of humans, we are not satiated by your peerless beauty.
From the lotus pond, they flow through the air.
There are many garlands and numerous white lotuses;
these trees are always laden with fruit,
and their exceedingly fragrant scents waft abroad.
There were pillars made of beryl rising a hundred [fathoms] high,
with long beams of crystal and ruby,
together with emeralds and red pearls.
These pillars are composed of the essence of light.
Above them stands this excellent celestial mansion, possessing a thousand pillars and incomparable majesty.
The second jewel is a golden pedestal,
well-covered with excellent bands of refined gold,
highly polished and made of pure Jambūnada gold.
Endowed with a palace, stairs, and a terrace;
firm, lovely, and well-proportioned,
it is exceedingly worthy of contemplation and charming.
In Ratanantara there was abundant food and drink,
surrounded by throngs of celestial nymphs,
resounding with the music of muraja drums, ālambara lutes, and various instruments.
You have been saluted with hymns of praise and veneration.
You rejoice, O awakener of the throngs of women,
in this most delightful and excellent celestial palace and mansion.
Inconceivable, endowed with all virtues,
like King Vessavaṇa in the lotus grove;
was he a deva, or one who dwells in the waters, or a yakkha?
"Or are you a lord of the gods who has become a human?
The merchant caravan leaders ask you:
'Tell us, what is your name, O yakkha?'"
“I am a yakkha named Serīsaka,
guarding the path through the forest in the wilderness;
I protect this region.”
“O you who carry out the commands of King Vessavaṇa!
[The yakṣa replied: “Was this obtained by chance, or born of transformation, or was it made by yourself, or given by the gods?”
The merchant caravan leaders asked him:
“How was this delightful thing obtained by you?
“It was not obtained by overreaching, nor was it born of transformation.”
"This was not made by myself, nor was it given by the gods;
through my own non-evil deeds,
through my merits, this delightful thing has been obtained by me."
“What is your vow, and what indeed is your holy life?
Of what well-practiced deed is this the result?
The merchant caravan-leaders ask you this.”
"How was this celestial mansion obtained by you?
"When I ruled as king of the Kosalans, 'Pāyāsi' was my title."
At that time, I was one who held the view of nihilism, miserly, of evil character, and an advocate of annihilationism.
But there was also the ascetic Kumārakassapa.
He was learned, eloquent, and sublime;
he then delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to me,
dispelling my doubts regarding various views.
Having heard that discourse on the Dhamma from him,
I declared myself a lay follower;
I abstained from taking life.
In this world, I shall avoid taking what is not given;
I shall drink no intoxicants, nor shall I speak falsehood,
and I shall be content with my own wife.
That was my vow, and that was my holy life;
this is the fruit of that well-practiced conduct.
By those very same blameless deeds, [I have attained this].
“By means of my merits, this celestial mansion has been obtained by me.
“Truly indeed have the wise men spoken;
the word of the learned is not otherwise.”
Wherever one who has performed meritorious deeds goes,
there he rejoices, seeking his desires.
Wherever there is sorrow and lamentation, [there he does not go].
Slaughter, bondage, and affliction—
wherever he goes, the doer of evil deeds never escapes from the miserable states of existence.
The people became as if utterly bewildered;
in this very moment, they were as if turned to a mass of froth—
both these folk and you yourself, O Prince.
“By what means, dear ones, did this fragrance arise?
“These Sirīsa trees, dear ones, emit divine,
sweet-smelling, and fragrant scents.”
They enter this celestial mansion,
dispelling darkness both by day and by night; yet,
only after the passing of these hundred years, do they [re-enter].
Each blister bursts one by one;
a hundred human years have passed since I was first reborn here in this body.
Having seen this, O dear ones, after remaining in this celestial mansion for five hundred years,
I shall pass away through the exhaustion of my lifespan and the exhaustion of my merit.
“I am utterly bewildered by that very grief.
“How could such a one as he grieve,
having obtained for a long time an incomparable celestial mansion?”
"And those who have been reborn for only a short time—
surely they of little merit would grieve.
"That advice of yours was indeed appropriate and worthy of me."
"Since you address me with such kind words,
my dear sons, you are protected by me;
go wherever you wish and fare well."
“Having gone to the land of Sindhu and Sovīra,
seeking wealth and longing for gain,
we applied ourselves with effort and fulfilled our generosity.”
“We shall perform a great Serīsaka festival.
“Do not hold a Serīsaka festival;
everything you propose shall be granted to you.”
Avoid evil deeds and resolve upon devotion to the Dhamma.
There is a lay follower in this Saṅgha.
One who is learned, endowed with virtue and conduct,
faithful, generous, and kind,
discerning, contented, and wise.
Perceiving things as they truly are, one should not speak falsely;
one should not intend harm to others;
one should not engage in divisive speech intended to create discord.
One should speak words that are gentle and kindly.
Being respectful, deferential, and disciplined,
one is free from evil and purified in higher virtue.
Thus a person, acting with noble conduct,
supports both mother and father in accordance with the Dhamma;
I believe it is for the sake of his parents that he does so.
He seeks enjoyments not for his own sake, but who,
after the passing of his mother and father,
will live the holy life inclined toward renunciation.
Upright, uncrooked, without guile, and without deceit,
one should not speak with a hint of artifice;
such a person, performing deeds well done, [is truly wise].
"How could one established in the Dhamma experience suffering?
It was for this reason that I revealed myself;
therefore, O merchants, behold the Dhamma!
Except for him who would here reduce it to ashes—
blind, bewildered, and lost in the forest—
he would be swiftly overcome by another.
“Happy indeed is the meeting with a true person.
“What is his name, and what work does he do?
What is his designation, and what is his clan?”
“We too, O yakkha, desire to see him for whose sake you have come here out of compassion;
it is indeed a gain for him whom you hold in such regard.”
“He who is a barber by name,
an upāsaka living on the fruit of his combing—
know him to be your messenger.”
"Do not despise him, for he is very dear.
"We know what you say, O yakkha, but we do not know that he is such as this."
“We too shall worship him, O Yakkha,
having heard your sublime words.
“Whatever people there are in this caravan...”
"Whether they be small, great, or even middling—
let them all take hold of this celestial mansion and let even the stingy behold the fruit of meritorious deeds."
There, they all said, "I was first," and having placed that barber at their head,
they all supported themselves upon that celestial mansion.
Like Masakkasāra to Vāsava,
they all there proclaimed their status as lay followers, each saying, "I was first."
They abstained from taking life,
they avoided what was not given in the world;
they did not drink intoxicants, nor did they speak falsehoods.
They were satisfied with their own wives and children.
There, they all declared themselves lay followers, each saying, "I first."
The caravan set out, offering its thanks,
repeatedly permitted by the power of the yakkha’s magic.
Having traveled, they reached the lands of the Sindhuvīras.
Seeking wealth and hoping for gain,
they returned safely to Pāṭaliputta with their profits complete, according to their efforts.
Having traveled safely through the assembly,
accompanied by their sons and wives,
they were joyful, elated, cheerful, and full of delight.
They performed a magnificent festival for the *serīsa* tree;
they had them construct a monastery cell (*pariveṇa*) for the *serīsa*.
Such is the service rendered to true persons (*sappurisa*).
The cultivation of the qualities of the Dhamma is of great benefit;
for the sake of one lay follower,
all beings indeed became happy.
The Serīsaka Vimāna is the tenth.
